source: Smyth and Keane (1995) Remembering to forget: a competence-preserving case deletion policy for CBR systems (IJCAI-95)
finding: Frames case deletion as a response to the utility (swamping) problem. Selective retention filters remove items for good, unlike selective utilisation filters that only hide them. Claims that classic deletion keeps speed in check but can cut competence.
numbers: Not numeric. Competence is the share of target problems the system can solve.
quote: Traditional deletion strategies will keep performance in check ... but they may cause problems for CBR system competence
limits: Position paper plus one small experiment.
agent_relevance: Pruning a memory for speed can silently remove the only case that solves some problem. A prune rule must protect coverage, not only cheap retrieval.

source: Smyth and Keane (1995) Remembering to forget: a competence-preserving case deletion policy for CBR systems (IJCAI-95)
finding: Formal competence model. Coverage(c) is the set of targets c solves. Reachable(c) is the set of cases that solve c. Cases fall into four classes: pivotal (reachable by no other case), auxiliary (coverage fully inside another case's), spanning (links regions covered by others), support (groups of cases with equal coverage).
numbers: Pivotal: Reachable(c) minus {c} is empty. Auxiliary: some other reachable case has a superset of its coverage. Support group: all members share the same coverage; removing one or more but not all loses nothing.
limits: Coverage and reachability are estimated from the case base itself, so the model assumes the case base mirrors the real problem distribution. Costly to compute (done once as start-up cost); updated with cheap heuristics (Algorithms 1 and 2) that are estimates.
agent_relevance: Gives a vocabulary for our subgoal library: a solved subgoal is pivotal if no other stored subgoal could have solved the same problem. Keep pivots, dedupe support groups, drop auxiliaries.

source: Smyth and Keane (1995) Remembering to forget: a competence-preserving case deletion policy for CBR systems (IJCAI-95)
finding: Footprint deletion (FD): delete auxiliary cases first, then support (from the largest group), then spanning, then pivotal. Footprint-utility deletion (FUD) uses a utility score only to break ties inside a class. The competence footprint is the smallest set with the same competence as the whole base.
numbers: Order: auxiliary, support, spanning, pivotal. If a pivot must go, pick the one with the largest reachable set or the least coverage.
limits: The authors note FD alone can keep low-utility cases and drop high-utility ones of equal class; hence FUD.
agent_relevance: Two-stage rule fits a scaffold: first protect irreplaceable items by coverage, then rank the rest by measured use.

source: Smyth and Keane (1995) Remembering to forget: a competence-preserving case deletion policy for CBR systems (IJCAI-95)
finding: Experiment 1. Property valuation CBR with nearest-neighbour retrieval. Start 50 cases, 160 target problems, swamping limit 75 cases. Benchmark competence 100% with no learning. Footprint policies held 100%. Random deletion ended at 86% and utility deletion at 80% of that level. Drop began about 25 trials after the limit was hit.
numbers: Initial base 50 cases; 160 targets; limit 75; final competence FD 100%, FUD 100%, random 86%, utility-only 80%.
quote: random deletion (RD) and utility deletion (UD) policies resulted in significant drops in competence
limits: One toy domain (residential property valuation), one run per policy as reported, no variance, no significance test.
agent_relevance: Plain utility-based pruning was worse than random deletion here. A utility score that ignores coverage can be the most harmful rule.

source: Smyth and Keane (1995) Remembering to forget: a competence-preserving case deletion policy for CBR systems (IJCAI-95)
finding: Experiment 2 and Table 1. The case base had 20 pivotal, 5 auxiliary, 25 support (in 7 support groups), 0 spanning cases. A competence-optimal base is all pivots plus one per support group, so 27 cases. With a limit just over 25 cases, FD and FUD reached about 90% of benchmark competence; random and utility reached about 60%.
numbers: Table 1: pivotal 20, auxiliary 5, support 25 (7 groups), spanning 0. Minimal base = 27 cases. At limit near 25: footprint about 90%, random and utility about 60%. Limit swept 5 to 95 cases.
limits: Same single domain; values read from the text and graph description, one run per curve.
agent_relevance: About half the stored cases (23 of 50) were redundant given the others. A dedupe pass by coverage could have almost halved memory at no cost to solved problems.

source: Smyth and Keane (1995) Remembering to forget: a competence-preserving case deletion policy for CBR systems (IJCAI-95)
finding: Authors state the main assumption and the risk: if the case distribution is not a good picture of the target distribution, the competence model is unreliable and the policy loses effect. They also suggest using the model when building the first case base, since irrelevant cases add noise to retrieval.
numbers: Assumption: case distribution approximates target distribution.
quote: If the case distribution is not a reliable estimate of the target distribution then the competence model will not be reliable.
limits: Authors call results preliminary. Never tested under distribution shift. Later work (Xiong et al. 2025, a17) tests shift for LLM agents.
agent_relevance: Deletion by coverage fails when tasks drift. For our agent, treat coverage estimates as stale when the problem mix changes.

source: Wilson and Martinez (2000) Reduction techniques for instance-based learning algorithms (Machine Learning 38:257-286)
finding: Survey plus new methods (DROP1 to DROP5, DEL) for removing stored instances from nearest-neighbour learners. Tested 16 reduction methods against plain kNN on 31 datasets with k=3, HVDM distance, 10-fold cross-validation, paired t-tests and a Wilcoxon test. Splits the methods into: historic (CNN, SNN, IB2), noise filters (ENN, RENN, All k-NN), aggressive reducers (ELGrow, Explore), and accurate reducers (IB3, DROP2-5, DEL).
numbers: 31 datasets; 10-fold CV; k=3; 16 reduction methods.
limits: Classification only, not problem solving. Class noise is the only noise type tested. No tuning of k per method.
agent_relevance: Closest large-scale measurement of how much memory can be dropped before accuracy falls. Gives the tradeoff curve we lack.

source: Wilson and Martinez (2000) Reduction techniques for instance-based learning algorithms (Machine Learning 38:257-286)
finding: Clean-data result. Average accuracy: kNN 82.11%. DROP2 81.07% with 14.03% of instances kept; DROP3 81.14% with 14.31%; DROP4 81.11% with 17.30%; DROP5 81.39% with 16.09%. CNN 76.48% (26.69% kept), IB2 76.58% (26.64%), IB3 78.85% (16.13%), DROP1 72.65% (8.41%).
numbers: kNN 82.11. DROP3 81.14 at 14.31% storage. DROP1 72.65 at 8.41%. Averages over 31 datasets.
limits: DROP2-5 lie within about 1 point of kNN on average. Individual datasets vary and some show significant losses.
agent_relevance: About 85% of stored items can go with about 1 point accuracy loss, if removal is order-aware (remove the item whose neighbours still classify correctly without it, checking against items already removed).

source: Wilson and Martinez (2000) Reduction techniques for instance-based learning algorithms (Machine Learning 38:257-286)
finding: Noise result. With 10% uniform class noise added, kNN fell from 82.11 to 78.93. DROP2-5 stayed above kNN: DROP2 79.99, DROP3 80.00, DROP4 79.57, DROP5 79.95, keeping 8 to 15% of data. CNN fell to 68.14 and IB2 to 67.80 and kept more.
numbers: Noisy accuracy: kNN 78.93; DROP3 80.00 (11.49% kept); CNN 68.14; IB2 67.80; All k-NN 79.98 (64.58% kept).
limits: Noise was random class flips on training data only. Real stored experiences carry structured, correlated errors (see a14).
agent_relevance: Pruning can raise accuracy when stored items are wrong. Keeping every attempt, including bad ones, is not neutral.

source: Wilson and Martinez (2000) Reduction techniques for instance-based learning algorithms (Machine Learning 38:257-286)
finding: Noise filters (ENN, RENN, All k-NN) keep over 75% of instances. In clean data they are slightly below kNN. With noise they beat kNN. All k-NN had best accuracy and lowest storage of the three under noise. ELGrow keeps about 1.8% of data but loses accuracy (75.68 clean). Explore keeps about 2% and reaches 79.24 clean, 77.96 noisy.
numbers: ELGrow 75.68 / 1.83% storage; Explore 79.24 / 2.01%; All k-NN clean 81.01 / 77.44%; ENN family keeps 75 to 83% clean.
limits: Averages hide dataset spread. DROP1 did worst of the DROP family because it ignored items already removed.
agent_relevance: Two different jobs: filter wrong items (keeps most of the base) versus compress redundant items (keeps a few percent). Do both, in that order.

source: Xiong et al. (2025) How memory management impacts LLM agents: an empirical study of experience-following behavior (arXiv 2505.16067v2)
finding: Tests memory addition rules on four agents (synthetic RegAgent, EHRAgent on MIMIC-III, AgentDriver on nuScenes, CIC-IoT Agent) with GPT-4o-mini as backbone. Add-all lowered results versus a fixed memory. Selecting what to add with a strict (ground-truth) judge raised results. Better judges helped more: a coarse GPT-4.1-mini judge fine-tuned on 300 trajectories (C3) nearly matched strict.
numbers: RegAgent success rate: fixed 67.53, add-all 55.48, C1 63.18, C2 65.78, C3 67.35, strict 70.95. EHRAgent accuracy: fixed 16.75, add-all 13.05, C1 26.19, C3 34.66, strict 38.50. AgentDriver success: fixed 40.11, add-all 32.32, strict 51.00. CIC-IoT: fixed 71.50, add-all 59.90, strict 85.40.
quote: a strict selective addition ... consistently yields superior performance
limits: Strict judge uses ground truth, not available in the wild. Judge-model quality drives everything. Single backbone for most runs. No variance reported in Table 1.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that storing every finished attempt can harm an agent. For a retain rule, a code-checked success signal beats an LLM self-grade. Add-all scored 9 to 15 points below strict.

source: Xiong et al. (2025) How memory management impacts LLM agents: an empirical study of experience-following behavior (arXiv 2505.16067v2)
finding: Names the experience-following property: when a task is similar to a retrieved record, the agent output copies that record's output. In RegAgent the correlation between input similarity and output similarity approaches Pearson r near 1 once memory is large. Fixed small memory showed lower similarity and the agent reasoned more instead of copying.
numbers: Pearson r about 1 between input and output similarity in RegAgent with growing memory.
limits: Measured on four agents with different similarity definitions (cosine on vectors, code-plagiarism score for EHRAgent).
agent_relevance: A memory that offers a near match makes the agent imitate it. A wrong near match is therefore worse than none; a harm case is a retrieved case that misleads.

source: Xiong et al. (2025) How memory management impacts LLM agents: an empirical study of experience-following behavior (arXiv 2505.16067v2)
finding: Error propagation: mistakes in stored records are copied into new runs, which are then stored. Gap against an error-free variant (same retrieved inputs, ground-truth outputs) opened at once and widened under add-all and coarse selection. With strict addition AgentDriver closed the gap and passed the error-free variant after about 2000 executions.
numbers: Gap grows over 2000 to 4000 executions; strict addition passes error-free memory after about 2000 runs in AgentDriver.
limits: Strict addition needs ground truth. The surpass result is for AgentDriver only.
agent_relevance: Errors compound through a retain loop. Retention needs a gate that does not rely on the model's own judgement (guardrails G2, G3).

source: Xiong et al. (2025) How memory management impacts LLM agents: an empirical study of experience-following behavior (arXiv 2505.16067v2)
finding: Deletion rules. Periodic deletion (drop records whose retrievals in a window fall below a threshold) cut memory by about 60 to 80% at small cost. History-based deletion (drop a record once it has been retrieved at least n=5 times and its mean downstream utility is below a threshold) gave the best accuracy with a strict judge. Combined rule gave the smallest memory.
limits: With the coarse C1 judge the picture is mixed: CIC-IoT 74.00 no deletion, 73.70 history, 68.80 combined. Gains depend on judge quality.
agent_relevance: Usage-then-utility pruning is workable: wait for enough retrievals, then drop records that did not help. About 75 to 80% fewer records at about equal accuracy (EHRAgent 1012 to 248 records, 38.67 to 42.34).

source: Xiong et al. (2025) How memory management impacts LLM agents: an empirical study of experience-following behavior (arXiv 2505.16067v2)
finding: Misaligned experience replay: records that passed the add filter can still mislead later runs. Records that history-based deletion removed had higher error than those retained, even under the strict filter. With an unfine-tuned GPT-4o-mini as the utility judge, deletion helped EHRAgent but hurt AgentDriver; fine-tuned judges were stable.
numbers: KDE plots of absolute error: deleted records sit at higher error than retained ones (RegAgent, record retrieved more than 5 times).
limits: Mechanism shown for the synthetic agent by error magnitude; for real agents the cause is argued, not isolated.
agent_relevance: A stored success is not automatically a useful example. Track per-record harm after the record is reused, not only whether the original run succeeded.

source: Xiong et al. (2025) How memory management impacts LLM agents: an empirical study of experience-following behavior (arXiv 2505.16067v2)
finding: Stress tests. Under task distribution shift, strict addition alone gave small gaps to the no-shift run and even beat it for AgentDriver; for EHRAgent history deletion fell below combined deletion, so periodic deletion helped stability. Under a hard cap equal to the initial memory (100 records for EHRAgent, 180 for AgentDriver), a combined rule that drops the lowest mean-utility record kept results above the fixed-memory baseline.
numbers: Caps of 100 and 180 records; performance converges as cap grows, so unbounded growth is not needed.
limits: Curves only (Fig 7, 17, 18); no table was read. Two agents.
agent_relevance: Gives a working design for a bounded library: periodic drop of unused items plus drop the lowest-utility item when over the cap.

source: Zhao et al. (2024) ExpeL: LLM agents are experiential learners (AAAI-24; arXiv 2308.10144)
finding: Maintains a list of text insights by editing operators: ADD, EDIT, UPVOTE, DOWNVOTE. A new insight starts at importance 2; upvote or edit raises the count; downvote lowers it; at zero it is removed. The authors say this protects against suboptimal successful trajectories. Successful trajectories are kept in a vector store and retrieved by task similarity.
numbers: New insight starts at importance 2; removal at 0. Ablation table 3 HotpotQA success: ReAct 28.0, hand-crafted insights 32.0, insights built with reflections 29.0, gpt-3.5 insights 32.0, full ExpeL 39.0. ALFWorld: ReAct 40.0, reasoning-similarity retrieval 48.5, random retrieval 42.5, task-similarity retrieval 59.0.
limits: Four-fold validation; standard errors shown. The importance-count rule itself is not ablated against no-pruning.
agent_relevance: A cheap vote-count rule for retiring bad insights. Retrieval by task similarity beat random retrieval by 16.5 points in ALFWorld, so what is retrieved matters more than how much is stored.

source: Zhao et al. (2024) ExpeL, experience volume and mode ablations
finding: More and more diverse experience raised results. Extraction from the few-shot examples alone gave no gain over ReAct. Diverse experience from Reflexion retries (failures and successes) beat experience from ReAct alone. Insights-only versus retrieval-only gave different winners by task.
numbers: HotpotQA insights-only 36% vs retrieval-only 31% vs full 39%; ALFWorld retrieval-only 55% vs insights-only 50% vs full 59%; WebShop 37% vs 38%.
limits: Text-only benchmarks; closed API models; authors say the insight list may need retrieval for lifelong use.
agent_relevance: Keeping failure and success pairs is useful as source material. Keep failure traces for abstraction even if they are not offered as examples.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Voyager: an open-ended embodied agent with large language models (arXiv 2305.16291)
finding: Skill library of verified code programs, stored by embedding of a description. A skill is added only after self-verification passes, within 4 refinement rounds. Library grows without pruning. Reported: 3.3x more unique items (63 items in 160 prompting iterations), up to 15.3x faster tech-tree milestones, 2.3x longer distances; without the skill library the agent plateaus in later stages.
numbers: 63 unique items in 160 iterations; 3.3x items, up to 15.3x tech-tree speed, 2.3x distance versus prior best. Random curriculum cuts items by 93%.
limits: No pruning or size ablation: nothing about when the library becomes too large. One environment (Minecraft), 3 runs per method in Table 1.
agent_relevance: Retain-on-verification is a good gate: only code that passed a check enters. Voyager did not test the cost of a growing library, so it gives no support for or against pruning.

source: Wang, Mao, Fried, Neubig (2024) Agent Workflow Memory (arXiv 2409.07429)
finding: Induces reusable workflows (abstracted sub-routines, example values replaced by placeholders such as product-name) from past runs, offline or online, and stores them separately. Relative success gains: 24.6% on Mind2Web and 51.1% on WebArena versus baselines. Online use needs no labelled data.
numbers: Relative gains 24.6% (Mind2Web) and 51.1% (WebArena); online beats baselines by 8.9 to 14.0 absolute points as train-test gaps widen. WebArena rule-based versus LM-based induction differ by 0.1 in success.
limits: Authors state that incorrect online workflows can lower scores.
agent_relevance: Abstracting a case into a reusable template is a form of dedupe: many near-equal runs collapse into one workflow.

source: Wang, Mao, Fried, Neubig (2024) Agent Workflow Memory, appendix quality analysis
finding: Proposes four memory-health metrics: number of workflows (fewer better), step coverage, function overlap between workflows (overlapping sub-trajectories), and utility rate (how often used). Neural induction yields 7.3 to 7.4 workflows per example. Combining offline and online workflows was not additive: offline workflows seemed to impair online ones and gave middling results.
numbers: Mind2Web step success, offline / online / both: cross-task 45.1 / 43.6 / 44.5; cross-website 33.7 / 33.9 / 33.3; cross-domain 32.6 / 35.5 / 34.1.
limits: Metrics are proposals; no study of pruning by these metrics.
agent_relevance: Ready-made health metrics for our library: size, overlap, coverage, use rate. Merging two memory sources can lower results.

source: Chhikara et al. (2025) Mem0: building production-ready AI agents with scalable long-term memory (arXiv 2504.19413)
finding: Memory update phase: for each extracted fact the system retrieves the top similar stored memories and asks an LLM tool-call to choose ADD, UPDATE, DELETE (contradicted) or NOOP. On the LOCOMO conversation benchmark Mem0 scores 26% relative better than the OpenAI memory on LLM-as-judge, with 91% lower p95 latency and over 90% fewer tokens than reading the full context.
numbers: 26% relative judge-score gain over OpenAI memory; p95 latency down 91% and token cost down over 90% versus full context; full context still highest J (about 73%).
limits: Full context still scored higher. The LLM chooses the operation, so errors in ADD/DELETE are unmeasured. No ablation of DELETE or NOOP alone was found in the text read.
agent_relevance: LLM-decided merge or delete is common practice but unvalidated. Our schema would use code checks (G5) for the same four operations.

source: Zhou et al. (2025) Memento: fine-tuning LLM agents without fine-tuning LLMs (arXiv 2508.16153)
finding: A case-based reasoning agent with an online-growing case bank of (state, action, reward) triples that keeps both successes and failures. Writes only the final step of each trajectory to avoid redundant storage. Retrieval count K tested at 0, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32: best at K=4, flat or slightly worse above. Authors conclude CBR needs a small, high-quality memory.
numbers: DeepResearcher average F1 / PM: K=0 59.9 / 72.2; K=4 64.5 / 78.5; K=8 64.1 / 78.2. Case bank over five iterations: non-parametric 79.84 to 84.85; parametric 80.46 to 85.44. GAIA validation 87.88%, test 79.40%.
limits: Case bank saturates at about 3k training tasks, so the authors could not find a point where growth hurt. No explicit deletion method. Iterations repeat the same task set.
agent_relevance: Offering 4 cases beat offering 8 to 32. A write-everything bank did not degrade in this finite setting, which differs from Xiong et al. (a12) and shows the effect depends on judge and task stream.

source: Zhong et al. (2024) MemoryBank: enhancing large language models with long-term memory (AAAI-24; arXiv 2305.10250)
finding: Forgetting rule from the Ebbinghaus curve: retention R = exp(-t/S). S starts at 1 on first mention, increases by 1 each time the memory is recalled, and time since recall t resets to 0. Recalled memories decay slower. Authors call it simplified and exploratory.
numbers: SiliconFriend retrieval accuracy: English ChatGLM 0.809, BELLE 0.814, ChatGPT 0.763; Chinese 0.84, 0.856, 0.711. Response correctness ChatGPT 0.716 (EN) and 0.655 (ZH).
limits: No ablation with versus without forgetting was seen in the text read, so the benefit of the forgetting rule is not isolated. Conversations are synthetic. Companion chat, not task solving.
agent_relevance: Use-based decay is a popular heuristic with no tested gain over simply keeping everything. Do not adopt on its authority.

source: Park et al. (2023) Generative agents: interactive simulacra of human behavior (UIST-23; arXiv 2304.03442)
finding: Keeps every observation in a memory stream and never deletes. Retrieval score is recency + relevance + importance, each min-max scaled to [0,1], all weights 1; recency decays 0.995 per sandbox hour since last retrieval; importance is an LLM 1-10 rating made at write time. Reflections are higher-level memories that cite their sources. Ablating memory components lowered believability.
numbers: TrueSkill mu: full 29.89 (sigma 0.72); no reflection 26.88; no reflection or planning 25.64; human crowdworkers 22.95; no memory, planning or reflection 21.21. Kruskal-Wallis H(4)=150.29, p<0.001; 100 participants.
limits: Measures believability judged by people, not correctness. No deletion, so no evidence on pruning.
agent_relevance: Scoring a memory at read time (recency, relevance, importance) is a soft alternative to deleting. Pruning is replaced by ranking.

source: Minton (1990) Quantitative results concerning the utility of explanation-based learning (Artificial Intelligence 42)
finding: [M, not opened] The origin of the utility problem: learned control rules in PRODIGY cost more in matching time than they saved in search, so a system that learned more could solve problems more slowly.
numbers: Not verified this session.
limits: Recalled from memory; do not cite numbers.
agent_relevance: Same trap for any library of retrievable cases: retrieval cost and distraction can outweigh gain.

source: Leake and Wilson (1998) Categorizing case-base maintenance: dimensions and directions (EWCBR-98)
finding: [M, not opened] Defines case-base maintenance as policies that revise the organisation or content of the case base to ease later reasoning. Classifies policies on dimensions such as when maintenance is triggered, type of change (index versus content), on-line versus off-line application, and scope.
numbers: Not verified this session.
limits: Recalled from memory; exact dimension names may differ.
agent_relevance: A taxonomy to cover our retain rule: trigger (on a signal, G1), scope (one item or the whole library), timing.

source: Smyth and McKenna (1999) Building compact competent case-bases (ICCBR) and McKenna and Smyth (2000) Competence-guided editing methods for lazy learning (ECAI)
finding: [M, not opened] Extended the 1995 competence model with coverage groups and relative coverage. Editing methods build a compact base by adding cases in order of competence contribution, and were compared with CNN, RENN and IB3 style editors.
numbers: Not verified this session.
limits: Recalled from memory; numbers not recorded.
agent_relevance: Constructive editing (add the next most useful case) as an alternative to destructive deletion.

source: Brighton and Mellish (2002) Advances in instance selection for instance-based learning algorithms (Data Mining and Knowledge Discovery 6)
finding: [M, not opened] Iterative case filtering (ICF) uses reachability and coverage sets like the 1995 model, with noise removal first, and was compared against RENN, DROP and others. Seen only as a search listing (614 citations per Semantic Scholar).
numbers: Not verified this session.
limits: Recalled from memory; do not cite numbers.
agent_relevance: Confirms the pattern from a07-a10: remove noise first, then compress redundancy by coverage.

source: Leake and Schack (2018) Exploration vs. exploitation in case-base maintenance: leveraging competence-based deletion with ghost cases (ICCBR)
finding: [M, title only from a Semantic Scholar listing] Likely keeps a record of deleted cases (ghost cases) to test later whether a deletion cost anything. Method inferred from the title; verify before use.
numbers: Not verified this session.
limits: Only the title was seen.
agent_relevance: Ghost records of pruned items, checked at retrieval time, would give a measured harm-of-deletion signal.
